what_it_does: Ray tracing is a rendering technique that simulates how light bounces around a 3D scene by casting millions of virtual rays and testing them against geometry. The geometry is organized into a tree structure called a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) — a nested set of boxes that lets the hardware quickly rule out most geometry without testing every triangle. Each box is normally stored as 32-bit floating-point numbers, which consumes a lot of memory bandwidth from main memory (a large, slow chip called DRAM). AQB8 compresses those bounding boxes down to 8-bit integers at every level of the tree and — crucially — redesigns the intersection test so it works directly on those small integers without first converting back to 32-bit. This simultaneously cuts the memory traffic and replaces expensive floating-point arithmetic units with much smaller integer units. A hierarchical error-compensation scheme ensures the approximation never causes a ray to miss a box it should have hit.
